To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

NK cells from the liver and spleen express lower levels of the glucose transporter Glut1 than NK cells from peripheral circulation, whereas NK cells from liver and spleen show higher expression of the amino acid transporters CD98 and CD98 than peripheral NK cells.

NK cell subsets from paired blood-livers and spleen-blood differ in their expression of the nutrient receptor Glut1, and the amino acid receptor CD98, and that the expression of these receptors is modulated following cytokine stimulation.
NK cells differ in expression of nutrient transporters depending on their tissue of origin.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how NK cells adapt to their microenvironment and how they are able to respond adequately.
the metabolic adaptation of human tissue-resident NK cells.

NK cell subsets in the peripheral blood and in tissues and their expression of the nutrient receptor Glut1, the amino acid transporter SLC3A2 (CD98) and the iron transporter transferrin receptor CD71.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
NK cells are able to adjust their expression of nutrient transporters to the local environment.
tissue-resident NK cells express lower levels of Glu1 and CD98, and higher levels of CD71, compared to blood-derived NK cells.
NK cells from different tissue compartments express different nutrient transporters, which may contribute to the functional differences observed for NK cells from different compartments.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the expression of the nutrient transporter CD98 on NK cells is regulated by cytokines and is differentially regulated on tissue-resident NK cells compared to CD56bright NK in the peripheral blood.
the expression of nutrient transporters is regulated by the microenvironment and that NK cell subsets differ in their expression of these transporters.
NK cells from blood, liver and spleen differ in their expression of nutrient transporters.
The main takeaway from our work is that
tissue-resident NK cells have a different metabolic profile than NK cells in the peripheral blood.
the metabolic requirements of NK cell subsets are not only regulated by cytokines, but also by the local microenvironment.
NK cell subsets differ in their metabolic requirements, and that these differences are not only reflected at the transcriptional level, but also at the protein level.
